newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers dig in as talks fail, again.
newsitem.headline: French truckers dig in as talks fail, again.

text.p: French truckers on Saturday saw no let-up in a six-day-old blockade of about 30 towns, and a dozen petrol depots, after unions and haulage bosses broke off talks.
"No date has been set for a resumption of talks," a company official told reporters after the failure of the third round in a marathon attempt to lift pressure weighing on the economy.
Government representative Robert Cros said Transport Minister Bernard Pons would meet the unions at their demand, for the first time since the dispute began, at nine p.m. (2000 GMT).
Unions said haulage bosses had made no new proposals, and urged the government to intervene.
"If the bosses don't shift their stance, as early as Monday we will restart the kinds of actions we have taken this week," said Christian Laflaquiere of the pro-Socialist CFDT union.

The companies have agreed to allow truckers to retire at 55 instead of 60, but they want the state to foot the bill. Unions say talks are stuck over the issues of working hours and payment for all working hours, including time spent loading.

Haunted by memories of a damaging 24-day rail strike a year ago which badly dented his popularity, Prime Minister Alain Juppe has called on both sides to end the dispute quickly and agreed that a Transport Ministry official chair the talks.

North of the south-western city of Bordeaux, which has Juppe as its mayor and is singled out for the toughest protests, truckers set up a new blockade on the A10 highway after letting dozens of exhausted Spanish, Portuguese, German and British colleagues through overnight.
Since Friday evening, truckers have virtually blocked a highway to Paris's wholesale food market at Rungis. Police said produce was getting through.

Tens of thousands of trucks blocked main roads and a dozen fuel depots. The southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit. Petrol stations ran out of fuel in areas of Normandy and in Bordeaux.
Unions say they would blockade Paris only as a last resort.
"Everything has yet to be negotiated -- working hours and wages are the biggest issues. The bosses have offered nothing," Joel Lecocq of the CFDT union told reporters before the talks.
Unions said the government had agreed to finance early retirement for truckers but only on condition the talks succeed on all other sticking points.

Thousands of foreign truck drivers, mostly British and Spanish forced to drive through France between northern and southern Europe, were stranded in the roadblocks, sleeping in their cabs and running out of food and money.

The Foreign Office in London ordered consulates in France to help stranded British drivers with money and making contact with home. The Spanish embassy advised drivers to lodge complaints with police so that they would be able to claim compensation for rotting cargoes.
More than 1,000 British truck drivers were stuck in blockades across France and British freight operators said the dispute was ruining them.
In France, the Association of Food Industry said the protest was starting to weigh on the industry's logistics.
Opposition Socialist leader sided with the truckers, who say they are underpaid and overworked due to cut-throat competition between companies.
